( ) Studies e cluded because of overlapping data or missing effect si e information ( 10) Studies e cluded because of overlapping data or missing effect si e information 7) ffect si e information provided by authors ( 12) Coding Procedure Coding followed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, we evaluated the studies' eligibility for inclusion based on titles and abstracts. In Step 2, we evaluated eligibility for inclusion based on full texts. Eligibility screening was done by three independent, trained coders (one professor, one post-doc, and one graduate student). In both steps, 100 studies were doublecoded to examine intercoder agreement (89% in Step 1 and 93% in Step 2).

For studies eligible for inclusion, we extracted information on the sample, the personality trait assessment, and the effect sizes. Regarding the sample, we coded the country of data collection, whether the sample was representative, the percentage of female participants, and the ethnicity of participants. Regarding the personality trait measure, we coded the name of the measure and the assessed trait, whether a measure was designed to assess the Big Five personality traits, its reliability, whether it assessed a broad or a narrow trait, the mode of assessment (i.e., self-report vs. other-report), and whether it assessed a maladaptive trait or not. Furthermore, as done by Bleidorn et al. (2022), we assigned each trait to the Big Five domains based on their correlations. For all measures that were not designed to capture the Big Five personality traits, we looked for empirically published correlations between these measures and established measures of the Big Five (see the coding instructions for details). Finally, regarding the effect size information, we coded the sample size at baseline, the age at baseline, the mean-level of a trait at baseline and at follow-up, the standard deviation of a trait at baseline and at follow-up, the time lag between assessments, and the test-retest correlation. We did not conduct a quality rating of the included primary studies but instead used relevant sample and assessment characteristics (e.g., the reliability of the measure, the representativeness of the sample) as meta-analytic moderators in our analyses (see below for details).

Data extraction of eligible articles was done by four independent, trained coders and 55% of studies were double coded. Intercoder agreement ranged from 82% for whether a trait was maladaptive to 100% for test-retest correlations, with an overall agreement of 96%.

Divergent coding was resolved through discussion. More details on the coding procedure can be found in the coding instructions uploaded to OSF (https://osf.io/qdnyk).

Data Analysis

Data analysis was conducted in R (Version 4.3.2) using the R package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010). Generally, our meta-analytic procedure closely followed the analysis strategy of Bleidorn et al. (2022) to obtain comparable results. We conducted joint metaanalyses including data from all three sources (our new dataset, the dataset of Bleidorn and colleagues, and the dataset of Roberts and colleagues) 1.

Calculation of Effect Sizes

Our effect size of interest was the variability ratio introduced by Nakagawa et al.

(2015). This coefficient was initially developed to quantify whether the variability differs between two independent groups. However, the equations have been modified to be applied to a within-person context by accounting for the correlation of assessments when calculating its sampling variance (Senior et al., 2020; Viechtbauer, 2010). Based on the standard deviation of a trait at baseline (SD1) and the standard deviation of a trait at follow-up (SD2), the variability ratio can be calculated as follows: (1) 𝑉𝑅 = 𝑙𝑛 ( 𝑆𝐷 2 𝑆𝐷 1 ) 1 We had preregistered to conduct the analyses of the methodological moderators beyond age and time lag without the dataset of Roberts et al. (2006) as the moderators have not been extracted (in the same way) by these authors.

However, during our coding process, we decided to add codings of the methodological moderators to the dataset of Roberts et al. (2006) to be as comprehensive as possible with our meta-analysis. Thus, we were able to use all three data sources for all analyses.

Using the logarithmic transformation ensures that the effect size is symmetrically distributed and that the sampling distribution is closer to normality. For interpretation purposes, we backtransformed the variability ratio after conducting the meta-analyses. After back- transformation, values smaller than 1 indicate that the variance or standard deviation (SD) of personality traits decreased over time (SD2 < SD1), whereas values larger than 1 indicate that the variance of personality traits increased (SD2 > SD1).

The sampling variance of the variability ratio can be calculated as follows, with r being the test-retest correlation and n2 being the sample size at T2 (Senior et al., 2020; Viechtbauer, 2010): (2) 𝑠 𝑉𝑅foot_0 = 1-𝑟 2 𝑛 2 -1

We used the escalc-function from the metafor package to compute the effect size and sampling variance. If the test-retest correlation of a personality trait was missing for a certain sample, we imputed this correlation based on the results on rank-order stability of personality traits by Bleidorn et al. (2022) 2.

Meta-Analytic Strategy

We conducted random-effects meta-analyses using a meta-regression framework. We weighted the effect sizes by the inverse of the sampling variance so that effect sizes that are estimated with a higher precision received more weight in the analyses. To deal with the dependency of effect sizes, we used a three-step procedure as recommended by Viechtbauer (2010) and Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022). First, we estimated the approximate variancecovariance matrix of dependent effect sizes using the vcalc()-function. This function approximates the variance-covariance matrix of effect sizes based on assumptions on their dependencies. In our case, we accounted for dependencies due to different traits included in the same sample, for dependencies due to multiple assessments of the same sample (i.e., when a study had three or more assessment waves), and for dependencies due to different assessment modes in the same sample. Based on meta-analytic findings on personality traits, we assumed a correlation of 1 = .48 for different traits belonging to the same Big Five domain such as grit and self-discipline belonging to the domain conscientiousness (Pace & Brannick, 2010), an auto-correlation of  = .61 for multiple assessments belonging to the same sample (Bleidorn et al., 2022), and a correlation of 2 = .55 for different assessments modes within the same sample (Connolly et al., 2007). Second, using this approximative variance-covariance matrix, we estimated a multilevel meta-analytic model using the rma.mv()-function with effect sizes nested in studies. Finally, using the robust()-function, we estimated cluster-robust standard errors as implemented in the R package clubSandwich

Age and Time Lag as Predictors

As a first step, we included age and time lag between assessments as predictors of the variability ratio to examine how the variance of personality traits changes across the lifespan while controlling for different time lags between assessments. We estimated separate metaanalyses for the different Big Five traits.

For time lag, we subtracted 1 from the original time lag so that a value of 0 corresponds to a time lag of 1 year. Thus, the intercept in the meta-analytic models describes changes in the variance of personality traits over a time lag of 1 year. Using this procedure, our meta-analysis provides estimates that are comparable to meta-analyses on the lifespan development of other constructs, which estimated yearly change rates (e.g., Buecker et al., 2023; Bühler et al., 2021; Orth et al., 2018).

For age, we tested different functional forms of the relationship between age and changes in the variance of personality traits using a piecewise regression approach similar to the procedure described in Bleidorn et al. (2022) and Briley and Tucker-Drob (2014).

To do this, we divided the linear age variable into different age bins and compared models for differently created age bins. Generally, creating age bins means that the age information is divided into several variables so that these bins can differ in their association with the variability ratio. For example, dividing a linear age variable into two age bins-one covering age 1 to 40 and one covering age 41 to 80-would allow to reflect increases in the variability ratio in the first half of life but decreases in the variability ratio in the second half. There are many possible ways to split a linear age variable into age bins, and this categorization is always to some degree arbitrary. The advantage of the piecewise regression approach is that it allows to compare meta-analytic models with differently created age bins. As the most fine-grained categorization, we started by splitting the age variable into 5-year age bins (e.g., 1-5, 6-10, 11-15) including a catchall bin for people over 75 years to ensure sufficient sample size in each age bin. For example, for a sample with a mean age of 22 years, splitting the age information into 5-year age bins results in a value of 5 for the first four age bins (1-5 years, 6-10 years, 11-15 years, and 16-20 years), a value of 2 in the fifth age bin (i.e., 21-25 years), and a value of 0 for all remaining age bins. Then, we summarized certain age bins to examine whether imposing the same trajectory for larger age groups reduced model fit or not. For example, we summarized the age bins 6-10 years and 11-15 years to a combined age bin 6-15 years to test whether these age groups develop similarly in their variability ratio. We estimated and compared all possible combinations of separating and summarizing age bins between the simplest model (just one age bin = the linear time variable) and the most complex model (16 separate 5-year age bins). In total, we estimated and compared 32,768 models for each trait. To identify the best-fitting model, we inspected the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), which allowed us to compare the fit of non-nested models. AIC and BIC are model comparison criteria that balance goodness of fit against model complexity, with lower values indicating a better tradeoff (Chakrabarti & Ghosh, 2011).

The model with the lowest AIC and BIC was selected as best-fitting piecewise model (see Section 4 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef for details). However, we also inspected and compared the ten models with the lowest AIC and BIC for each trait to examine whether age shows similar relations to changes in the variance of personality traits across traits.

Further Moderation Analyses

To test whether other sample characteristics, study characteristics, or measurement characteristics are related to changes in the variance of personality traits, we included further moderators into the best-fitting model selected in the previous step. We tested the publication year, the reliability of a trait measure, the percentage of female participants in a sample, and mean-level changes in the measure as continuous moderators. Furthermore, as categorical moderators, we tested the mode of report (self, other), whether a construct was assessed broadly or narrowly (broad, facet), whether a measure was designed to measure the Big Five personality traits (no, yes), whether a measure assessed maladaptive traits (no, yes), the region of data collection (North America, Asia, Global South, Northern Europe, Southern Europe), whether a sample was representative (no, yes), and whether a construct was assessed in a reversed coded fashion (no, yes).

We centered all metric moderators (except mean-level changes, which we coded as

Cohen's d) and used dummy coding for all categorical moderators. The category that was named first in the section above was used as reference category. We included moderators separately into this best-fitting piecewise model but also estimated an overall model including all moderators.

Publication Bias

We expected publication bias not to be a substantial problem in the present metaanalysis, as most included studies were not designed to examine changes in personality trait variance. Nonetheless, we used multiple strategies to evaluate publication bias. First, we estimated the PET model by regressing effect sizes on their standard errors. The intercept represents the estimated effect as sampling variance approaches zero (i.e., as sample size approaches infinity). If the PET intercept is statistically significant, the PEESE model-using the squared standard error (variance) as predictor-was estimated, and its intercept is interpreted as the bias-corrected effect (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014). Second, we used the trim and fill method to investigate whether there are missing effect sizes at one side of the funnel plot (Duval & Tweedie, 2000). A high number of missing effect sizes would indicate publication bias. Third, we used the test of excess significance, which compares the observed number of significant findings to the expected number of significant findings (Ioannidis & Trikalinos, 2007). If the number of observed significant findings is substantially higher than the number of expected significant findings, this would be an indication of publication bias.

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Across all three literature searches (Roberts, Bleidorn, and new search), 362 studies with 4,071 effect sizes were included in the present meta-analysis. A table summarizing the characteristics of the included studies can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef. Most research available was on the Big Five trait of neuroticism (295 studies, 1547 effect sizes) and least on openness (132 studies, 543 effect sizes). Table 1 and Table 2 summarize descriptive statistics of relevant study characteristics merged across all three literature searches. The studies included in the present meta-analysis were published between

Changes in Personality Trait Variance Across Time and Age

To address our first research question regarding the development of personality trait variance across time and age, we examined various functional forms of the links between age and the variability ratio using a piecewise regression approach. This approach showed that, for all personality traits, simple models with few age predictors were preferred, indicating that the variability ratio was similar across the entire lifespan. For conscientiousness, a model with only one linear age variable covering the entire lifespan fitted the data best. For the other four traits a model with two age bins (Age 1-5, Age 5>) fit best. In the following, we only report the findings of the best-fitting model for each Big Five trait. Further details on the piecewise regression approach and results from alternative model specifications (i.e., with different age bins) can be found in Section 4 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef.

Table 3 provides an overview of the results of the best-fitting models with age and time as predictors for each personality trait. The time lag between assessments was unrelated to the variability ratio for all traits except extraversion, suggesting that changes in personality trait variance were largely independent from the time interval between assessments. For extraversion, a longer lag between assessments was associated with an increase in personality trait variance (b = 0.004, p = .043).

Regarding age, we found a few significant effects. The development of the variability ratio across the lifespan for the different personality traits is depicted in Figure 3. This figure illustrates the expected changes in personality trait variance at a certain age over a time interval of 1 year. A variability ratio of 1 indicates that the variance of personality traits remains stable over 1 year, a variability ratio below 1 indicates that the variance decreases at a certain age, and a variability ratio above 1 indicates that the variance increases.

For agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness, the confidence intervals of the variability ratios included 1 throughout the entire lifespan, indicating that the variance of these personality traits is stable across age. A similar conclusion can be drawn for the other two personality traits-extraversion and neuroticism-albeit with some nuances. For extraversion, we found a variability ratio significantly below 1 for ages 45 to 80, suggesting that the variance of extraversion decreased in middle and old adulthood. For neuroticism, we found a variability ratio above 1 for ages 5 to 14. Thus, the variance of neuroticism seemed to increase in late childhood and early adolescence. However, for both traits, the meta-analytic effects pointed to variance changes of at most 1% to 2% per year.

Notably, there was a large heterogeneity of effect sizes (79% ≤ I² ≤ 90%), indicating that studies, samples, and measures differed in whether and how their variances changed over time. Prediction intervals can be used to further illustrate this heterogeneity, as they describe the range of expected variability ratios in a future study at a certain target age. For most target ages and traits, prediction intervals ranged from VR = 0.85 to 1.18, indicating that variance decreases by about 15% or increases by about 18% can be expected in a future study (see Section 4 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef for graphical illustrations).

In sum, changes in personality trait variance were largely independent from the time interval between assessment and the age of participants, suggesting remarkable stability of personality trait variance. However, there was substantial unexplained heterogeneity in the effect sizes. Thus, we next tested whether study, sample, and assessment characteristics were able to explain some of this heterogeneity. Note. Further Moderation Analyses

To address our second research question, we included study, sample, and assessment characteristics as moderators in the best-fitting models identified in the previous step. Results of these moderator analyses are summarized in Table 4.

There were some significant associations between the examined moderators and the variability ratio. For example, for agreeableness, a higher reliability was related to a lower variability ratio (b = -0.107, p = .037) and, for openness, the variability ratio was larger in representative samples (b = 0.022, p = .038). However, similar effects did not emerge for the other personality traits and in most cases the effects did not replicate when examining all moderators in a joint model (see Section 5 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef for details). The only exception from this pattern was the association between mean-level changes and the variability ratio for agreeableness and neuroticism. For these traits, mean-level increases were associated with a higher variability ratio suggesting that, when the mean-levels of these traits increased, their variance tended to increase as well, supporting the established mean-variance relationship (Nakagawa et al., 2015).

Furthermore, we examined whether the included moderators reduced the amount of unexplained heterogeneity. Generally, reliability and mean-level changes were associated with the largest reduction in I² values. For example, for conscientiousness, reliability of measures reduced the I² values from 89% to 83%. In models with all moderators combined I² values ranged from 76% for openness to 87% for agreeableness, suggesting that the considered study, sample, and assessment characteristics explained at least some of the observed heterogeneity (see Section 5 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef for more details). Publication Bias

We used different methods, including regression tests, trim and fill analysis, and tests of excess significance, to evaluate whether the findings of our meta-analysis were biased by publication practices. The results of these analyses are summarized in Section 6 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef. The different approaches consistently provided no evidence for the presence of publication bias.

Exploratory Robustness Check: Big Five Measures Only

In our main analysis, we included a broad range of trait measures to be as comprehensive as possible. However, a possible downside of this approach is that the included measures differed in their research traditions (e.g., theoretical conceptualizations) and psychometric properties (e.g., reliability). Although our moderator analyses identified only few significant moderators of the variability ratio, we further tested the robustness of our findings by repeating the above-described piecewise regression approach including only measures that were designed to assess the Big Five personality traits with an (marginally) acceptable reliability of Cronbach's α > .60. Details on this analysis can be found in Section 7 of the https://osf.io/qdnyk/files/6yjef.

The results of this robustness check largely replicated the findings from our main analysis, with the main conclusion being that the variance of personality traits tends to be stable across time and age. Furthermore, we replicated the increase of variance in neuroticism in late childhood and adolescence. In contrast, the variance decrease of extraversion in middle and late adulthood was not found, indicating that this finding may not be robust. Furthermore, the heterogeneity of effect sizes tended to be smaller in these analyses, ranging from I² = 69% for extraversion to I² = 79% for agreeableness. This suggests that the substantial heterogeneity found in our main analysis can at least partly be explained by the use of different measures.

For a measure designed to measure Big Five personality traits, prediction intervals indicated that variability ratios between 0.88 between 1.12 are expected for most target ages, corresponding to variance increases or decreases by about 12%.

Discussion

In contrast to the broad evidence for mean-level and rank-order changes of personality traits across time and age, there has been little research on changes in personality trait variance across the lifespan (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Mõttus et al., 2016 Mõttus et al., , 2017)). In the present meta-analysis, we aimed to close this research gap by meta-analytically integrating 4,071 effect sizes from over 350 longitudinal studies with data from a total of 398,124 participants.

The present results suggest that the variance of personality traits is remarkably stable across the lifespan (Figure 3). That is, at the population level, people neither become more different nor more alike as they age. Yet, there was a large heterogeneity of effect sizes, suggesting that variance changes differed across studies, samples, measures, or other factors. This heterogeneity could partly be explained by methodological moderators such as the reliability of personality trait assessments or whether a measure was designed to capture the Big Five personality traits.

The Stability of Personality Trait Variance

The main take-away of the present meta-analysis is that the variance of personality traits does not significantly change across the lifespan (Figure 3). This finding may be surprising given that other developmental indicators, such as the mean-levels and rank-orders of traits, undergo remarkable changes across the lifespan (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Borghuis et al., 2017; R. I. Damian et al., 2019; Seifert et al., 2024). Different theoretical and methodological reasons may explain the observed stability pattern.

Theoretical and Methodological Explanations

Although most personality development theories do not explicitly describe how the variance of personality traits is expected to change across the lifespan, the present findings align most closely with the Five-Factor Theory, which posits that personality development is largely completed by age 30 (McCrae & Costa, 2008). An alternative explanation would be that multiple processes leading to variance increases and decreases are at work that cancel each other out and thus lead to a stable pattern of personality variance across the lifespan.

Some scholars have suggested that corresponsive life experiences-people selecting into environments that match preexisting individual differences-may lead to an increase in personality trait variance (McCrae, 1993; Mõttus et al., 2016 Mõttus et al., , 2019)). In contrast, normative life experiences like transitioning into employment in young adulthood may trigger similar personality trait changes across people and predict a decrease in personality trait variance (Mõttus et al., 2016; A. J. Wright & Jackson, 2024). The observed stability of personality trait variance may, hence, imply that these different processes act together and counteract each other in shaping the development of personality trait variance (Roberts & Nickel, 2021).

Another explanation may be that the timing and effects of relevant developmental processes differ across individuals. Such idiosyncrasies in the timing and effects of the processes described in theories of personality development may explain that, at the population level, the extent of individual differences does not change across time and age (see Mõttus et al., 2016, for a similar hypothesis). If, for example, individuals differ in their timing of selecting into environments that strengthen pre-existing individual differences, these timingrelated differences could explain why we did not find any increases in personality trait variance at any particular age. Similarly, there is emerging evidence that people differ in their personality trajectories after important life experiences so that normative life events like graduation may not lead to a decrease in the variance of personality traits (Denissen et al., 2019; Haehner, Bleidorn, & Hopwood, 2024; Haehner, Wright, Krämer, et al., 2024; Schwaba et al., 2023). Such idiosyncratic effects of life events may be challenging to detect with common research designs, because complex constellations of risk factors may be responsible for these individual differences. To test these possibilities and examine more thoroughly how life events are related to variance changes, methods that can deal with high dimensional data like machine learning are needed (Bleidorn & Hopwood, 2019).

In addition to these theoretical explanations, the observed stability pattern may also have methodological reasons. For example, during classical item selection processes, items with a high between-person variance are typically preferred over items with a low variance, since items to which people respond differently are more diagnostically relevant for the assessment of the construct of interest (Moosbrugger & Kelava, 2020). Hence, the stability of personality trait variance could be explained by a ceiling effect. More generally, the use of Likert scales could itself limit personality trait variance, because only a limited number of response options is available to participants.

To test these alternative explanations about why the variance of personality traits remains stable across the lifespan, an experimental paradigm would be ideal that manipulates specific mechanisms of personality development such as selection into specific environments while also testing methodological factors (e.g., the number of response options or variance changes in specific items). To make such an experiment feasible, a reasonable first step would be to examine these processes at shorter time scales by zooming in on processes of situation selection and personality states in everyday life (Rauthmann et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2015). For example, future research could manipulate situation selection over a few days to examine whether there is an increase or decrease in the variance of personality states.

According to contemporary process theories of personality development, one could then expect that these state-level effects manifest as trait differences over time (Geukes et al., 2018; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).

Genetically-informed designs like twin studies are another promising way to investigate the mechanisms of changes in personality trait variance across the lifespan. For example, corresponsive processes-individuals selecting into environments that align with their dispositional traits-are expected to manifest as increases in the genetic component of personality trait variance over time, reflecting gene-environment correlations and transactional dynamics. In contrast, socialization forces may exert converging effects, pulling individuals toward similar developmental trajectories and thereby reducing environmental variance. If these counteracting forces are both active, one might observe a developmental shift in the structure of trait variance-with increasing genetic variance and increasing environmental variance-despite relatively stable total phenotypic variance. Such dynamic shifts were discussed by Mõttus et al. (2019), who emphasized the need to go beyond static estimates of heritability and instead consider how the relative contributions of genetic and environmental influences evolve over time.

In summary, the finding that the variance of personality traits remains fairly stable across the lifespan could be explained by theoretical and methodological reasons. However, the explanations for this stability remain largely speculative, outlining the necessity for future research and theory development to fully understand the ways in which personality traits develop across the lifespan (Bleidorn, 2024).

Implications for Theory and Research on Personality Development

Regardless of the specific reasons for the findings of the present meta-analysis, the stability of personality trait variance has important implications for theory and research on personality development.

First, the present meta-analysis helps to clarify conflicting empirical findings from the few primary studies that had examined changes in personality trait variance (Allemand et al., 2008; Mõttus et al., 2017 Mõttus et al., , 2019;; Olaru et al., 2024; Small et al., 2003). Our results show that the stability of personality trait variance extends across nearly the entire lifespan, holds across various methodological moderators such as the region of data collection or the sample type, and cannot be explained by a mere lack of power to detect such changes. As such, the present meta-analysis provides critical information for personality development theories most of which lack predictions about whether and how the variance of personality traits develops across the lifespan (Bleidorn, 2024). A comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon is essential for refining existing theories, which must explain the observed variance stability alongside mean-level and rank-order changes, accounting for both their regularities and deviations (Bleidorn, 2025; Eronen & Bringmann, 2021; Mõttus et al., 2019).

Second, the findings of the present meta-analysis help to contextualize the existing knowledge on mean-level changes in the Big Five personality traits. For instance, the observed mean-level increases in agreeableness, conscientiousness, or extraversion in young adulthood cannot just be explained by some individuals becoming more extreme in these traits as this would imply an increase in personality trait variance. Instead, the present findings rather suggest that the mean-level changes in personality traits are symmetrical on the population level, with a similar number of people becoming more and less extreme.

Furthermore, the stability of personality trait variance suggests that there are no overseen disruptive life phases of personality development, in which increases and decreases in the mean-levels of personality traits may cancel each other out.

Third, the present findings are practically relevant, because a trait's predictive validity depends in part on its variance in a population (Mõttus et al., 2016). The stability of personality trait variance implies that personality traits have a similar potential of predicting important life outcomes across the entire lifespan, as the variance of a trait is the decisive for identifying associations with other variables. This finding suggests that personality traits are of similar importance to describe and explain differences between people in different life phases.

Fourth, a stable variance of personality traits across the lifespan facilitates longitudinal comparisons of variance-dependent estimates such as heritabilites or intra-class correlations.

The heritability of a construct, for example, describes the proportion of genetically explained variance in the total variance in a given population (Visscher et al., 2008). A stable variance of personality traits across the lifespan thus facilitates the comparison of heritability estimates derived from different age groups.

Changes in the Variance of Extraversion and Neuroticism

Although time lag and participants' age were largely unrelated to the development of personality trait variance, there were some deviations from this general pattern that deserve attention.

Specifically, we found that the variance of neuroticism increased in late childhood and adolescence (age 5 to age 14), suggesting that children become more different in their neuroticism during this life phase. This finding is consistent with previous cross-sectional studies on changes in personality trait variance in late childhood and adolescence (Mõttus et al., 2017 (Mõttus et al., , 2019;; Soto et al., 2011). Although the present meta-analysis could not directly test the mechanisms of this variance increase, we offer some speculations. First, it could be that children differ in their adaptation to the transition to school or between schools. In this life phase, children learn to adapt to the demands of school life and find their place in a peer group (Ladd & Price, 1987; Latsch, 2018; Lohaus et al., 2004). Some children might easily adapt to these demands, whereas other children might need more time, so that neuroticism becomes more heterogenous in late childhood. Second, neuroticism is the Big Five trait with the strongest affective component (Wilt & Revelle, 2015). Thus, individual differences in the development of emotion regulation skills may be responsible for the variance increase for neuroticism. Third, differences in the timing of and reactions to puberty may contribute to increases in the variance of neuroticism during adolescence (e.g., Reynolds & Juvonen, 2012). Puberty marks a major developmental transition involving profound physical and biological changes, alongside emotional and social shifts (Susman & Rogol, 2004).

Adolescents may vary in both the timing of these changes and their capacity to cope with them, which could lead to greater variability in neuroticism.

Furthermore, we found a slight variance decrease for extraversion in middle and old adulthood, indicating that, during these life stages, people become more alike in their extraversion. A possible explanation for this variance decrease may be that social roles in middle and old adulthood require more similar levels of extraversion. For example, as people progress in their work life, behaving assertively becomes relevant for many people, potentially reducing individual differences in this facet of extraversion. At the same time, there may be fewer opportunities to show the sociable and excitement-seeking facets of extraversion, which may also lead to decreases in extraversion in middle and late adulthood.

However, it should be noted that the variance of extraversion decreased only very slightly (VR = 0.98 to 0.99) and was not found in our exploratory analyses focusing on the Big Five measures only.

Taken together, there are some nuances regarding the conclusion that the variance of personality traits is stable across the lifespan. Still, our results regarding changes in the variance of personality traits should be interpreted with caution in the light of the large heterogeneity of effect sizes that we discuss next.

Heterogeneity of Effect Sizes

A caveat to the conclusions on stability and changes of personality trait variance is that there was a high level of effect-size heterogeneity, suggesting that changes in personality trait variance differed across studies, samples, and measures. Prediction intervals indicated that decreases or increases in personality trait variance by about 15% can be expected for a future study. Thus, although age and time lag were largely unrelated to changes in personality trait variance in the population, it is difficult to draw precise conclusions about the development of personality trait variance in a specific sample and study.

Notably, a high level of effect size heterogeneity is not specific to the present metaanalysis, but appears to be common for research on longitudinal trait development. For example, I² values ranged from 95% to 97% in meta-analyses on rank-order and mean-level changes of personality traits (Bleidorn et al., 2022) foot_2 and from 73% to 99% in meta-analyses on mean-level changes of life satisfaction (Buecker et al., 2023).

Exploratory analyses indicated that this heterogeneity may be partly explained by the inclusion of a broad set of trait measures that differed in their research traditions (e.g., theoretical conceptualizations) and psychometric properties (e.g., reliability; Table 4).

Examining changes in personality trait variance in measures designed to capture Big Five traits with a sufficiently high reliability resulted in a lower-but still substantialheterogeneity of effect sizes (69% ≤ I² ≤ 79%). However, even within the set of Big Five measures, differences in assessment characteristics could be responsible for the observed

Relevance of Variance Changes for Psychological Science

Although variance changes provide unique insights into the development of a construct (see Figure 1), these changes have received considerably less research interest than mean-level changes across psychological disciplines (Mõttus et al., 2017; Nakagawa et al., 2015; Senior et al., 2020). Thus, investigating variance changes is a topic of relevance beyond Mund et al., 2020). These data sources could be used to expand our understanding of variance changes across psychological constructs.

By offering benchmarks for the comparison of effect size estimates, we hope to facilitate future research on variance changes across the lifespan. For personality traits, the meta-analytic effects pointed to variance changes of at most 1% to 2% per year, providing an example for constructs with highly stable variances. In contrast, psychotherapeutic research has shown that symptom variance increases by about 9% to 12% in response to treatment (Herzog & Kaiser, 2022; T. Kaiser et al., 2022). To facilitate further effect sizes comparisons, we developed a ShinyApp that allows researchers to calculate the variability ratio in a specific study and compare it with our meta-analytic estimates for specific sample and assessment characteristics (https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/VarianceChange/).

Limitations and Future Directions

The present meta-analysis provides new insights into personality development by examining changes in the variance of personality traits across the lifespan. We integrated data from nine decades of research and over 340,000 individuals using meta-analytic techniques.

However, the present study is not without limitations, outlining the necessity for future research.

First, although we integrated findings from 362 studies and combined three comprehensive literature searches, the number of effect sizes was still relatively low during some life phases. Specifically, as can be seen in Figure 3, more research on personality development in infancy and old adulthood seems necessary to draw robust conclusions on personality development across the entire lifespan.

Second, by examining changes in the personality trait variance using meta-analytic techniques, we were able to include primary longitudinal studies that were not explicitly designed to investigate changes in personality trait variance over time. As a consequence, we could not test potential mechanisms explaining stability or change of the variance of personality traits such as selection into new environments or reaction to normative life experiences. Future research on why the variance of personality traits remains relatively stable across the lifespan is thus needed. Such research should try to isolate different mechanisms for changes in the variance of personality traits that we discussed in the present study to come closer to a causal understanding of personality development. Specifically, examining whether and how life events are related to changes in personality trait variance seems to be an important direction for future research.

Third, although we examined a broad and theory-based selection of possible moderators, these variables explained only a minor proportion of the overall heterogeneity in effect sizes. The lack of findings may be partly explained by the fact that we were not able to test some additional relevant moderators such as the data collection year or ethnicity due to insufficient reporting of these characteristics in the included primary research. Changing reporting practice could enable such investigations in the future.

Fourth, the generalizability of the conclusions of the present meta-analysis depends on

the included primary research. The majority of the existing evidence stems from North America and Europe, with only few studies from Asia, Southern Europe, and the Global South. Our focus on studies written in English may have amplified this problem. Although our findings suggest that findings generalize across different regions of data collection, future research on personality development from all around the globe is needed to better understand the cross-cultural generalizability of personality development (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025; Henrich et al., 2010; Van De Vijver, 2013).

Conclusions

How does the variance of personality traits develop across the lifespan? In the present meta-analysis, we addressed this question by integrating evidence from 362 longitudinal studies spanning nine decades of research. Except for some changes in personality trait variance in adolescence, we found that that the variance of personality traits remains highly stable across the lifespan. This stability of personality trait variance has important implications for personality research as it helps to contextualize the observed mean-level changes and influences statistical modeling including questions of personality-outcome prediction. Furthermore, our results may spark theoretical advancements on personality development given that theoretical accounts need to offer precise explanations of why the mean-levels of personality traits change over time while the variance around these meanlevels remains relatively constant. At the same time, we also found a significant heterogeneity of effect sizes that calls for further research on the patterns and causes of variance changes in personality traits. Finally, by providing benchmark values for the comparison of effect sizes in future studies, we hope to contribute to more cumulative science on lifespan changes in variance in psychological constructs.

Figure1 inclusion criteria: (a) They had an empirical, quantitative design (i.e., we excluded reviews, comments, or qualitative studies). (b) They were conducted with human subjects. (c) They were written in English. (d) They used a longitudinal design (i.e., two or more assessments of the same sample). (e) The retest-interval was at least six months. (f) The study included a measure of personality traits.

As done byRoberts et al. (2006) andBleidorn et al. (2022), we included trait measures beyond those assessing the Big Five personality traits but excluded measures of affect, attitudes, cognitive functioning, intelligence, mood, self-esteem, sex role, and values. (g) The trait measure was identical across measurement occasions (e.g., in terms of the number of items or response scale). (h) The sample was nonclinical and not the focus of an intervention. (i) The sample was homogenous regarding age (SD of age at baseline ≤ 3 years). (j) The study reported sufficient (and consistent) information to compute effect sizes (SD of a trait at T1, SD of a trait at T2, age at baseline, time lag between assessments or age at T2, and N at T1). If a study was eligible for inclusion but relevant information for effect size calculation was missing, we contacted corresponding authors via email. Using this procedure, 12 additional datasets were retrieved that were included in the meta-analysis. (k) The dataset was not already included in the meta-analytic dataset. If two studies were based on the same dataset, we included the study with more comprehensive information on changes in the variance of personality traits (e.g., largest N, more measurement occasions, more trait measures). We checked whether studies relied on the same data within our new literature search and with the meta-analytic datasets ofBleidorn et al. (2022) andRoberts et al. (2006). As illustrated in Figure2, our updated literature search identified k = 1,376 records. Applying our inclusion criteria, k = 103 of these studies were included in the present metaanalysis. Furthermore, k = 77 records fromRoberts et al. (2006) and k = 182 records fromBleidorn et al. (2022) could be included. In total, these 362 studies provided 4,071 effect sizes on changes in personality trait variance.

Existing research indicates that different Big Five measures differ remarkably in their content and show only medium-sized convergent correlations (.31 ≤ r ≤ .56; Pace & Brannick, 2010). Thus, aiming for unification of measures to capture personality trait development may be a direction for future research(Elson et al., 2023).
